utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd ask the witness to stay out because, until I opened up an e-mail, I had no information about the document we were seeking as of yesterday. A request or, rather, the order of the Court was communicated immediately to the National Council for Cooperation. They have to act through the military. We remained available to receive anything basically all night. I had a few hours allocated to time when people should be asleep, but we made arrangements to cover the whole period between then and now. In the event, the field office of the OTP in Belgrade was informed at ten to nine this morning that the military have apparently found the material and are transporting it to Belgrade. The National Council for Cooperation hopes to have the document in their possession at about half past ten and will then notify the field office to collect it. So I'm afraid there's no way, in reality, that I'm going to be able to ask any questions based on that document today. It's highly likely that I'm going to want to ask some questions on the basis of it. This witness has covered an enormous amount of territory, and I'm going to have to be selective about the questions I ask of him in any event if I'm to keep cross-examination within reasonable bounds in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He may have to be recalled for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that there's going to be a case for recall of this witness, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can endeavour to ascertain whether he could be recalled for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning. I'm not available after 1.30 tomorrow, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are trying to determine whether it would be convenient -- if, after you've looked at the material, you find that it is necessary to cross-examine on it, we're trying to determine whether tomorrow is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should let the parties know that we have been considering a number of possibilities, and one of them is that, instead of sitting next week, Tuesday, we would sit tomorrow, so that next week we'd only sit two days. It seems possible. We are investigating it. Mr. Nice, perhaps in the circumstances, then you could bring your cross-examination to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Assuming that the document arrives at the time stated, and assuming it's 400 pages, the only way I'll be able to deal with it by tomorrow is by identifying the pages in which I have an interest and having them faxed here, or possibly, if it arrives early enough, putting the thing on a plane, which I think gets in at about midnight tonight, and working all night on it with a team of interpreters. It's going to be difficult even at the best, but you can be sure that I'll do whatever I can because having witnesses recalled is something that's unattractive to everyone and unhelpful. But I'll certainly -- we'll know by the end of the morning a little bit more about the logistics of the document -- dealing with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, how much more time do you anticipate?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from what may be contained in the diary -- in the notebook, I would hope to finish in this session, or just into the next session, because there's so much stuff he's tried to cover, or has covered. But certainly no more than that. I'd want to be done. I understand there's another witness ready to come in. It might turn up a great deal of material of interest to us, or nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if that were to happen, would you not be better holding your fire now? Because you've already used up, I would have thought, at least your allocation of time, if it was divided according to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I had thought of that as well, yes. That might well be preferable, in which case we could start with the next witness now. I would be very happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, Mr. Milosevic, we are going to interpose your next witness. And who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Krsman Jelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Sel must be advised that he should be available for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you stop, please. I'm not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order not to waste time, I would like to kindly ask you to have that board brought in, because General Jelic will be coming with maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Will the court deputy see to it that the easel is brought in, and the blackboard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Mr. Milosevic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Court deputy, will you see that the easel is brought in, and the blackboard. You may begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please introduce yourself and describe briefly your training and career.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: My name is Krsman Jelic. I am a major general, retired, born on the 7th of April, 1947, in Podujevo, Kosovo and Metohija, in the Republic of Serbia. I currently live in Nis. I'm married, father of three. Never convicted. After completing my high school in '66, I enrolled in the military academy, and further on, during my career, I completed all training courses available in the JNA and the army of Yugoslavia, including the highest level of education the School of National Defence in 1996. During my career I occupied mainly command positions, beginning with company commander, battalion commander, detachment commander, light brigade commander, armoured brigade commander, chief of staff of the Pristina Corps, commander of the Operative Group South during the attempts to resolve the crisis in the south of Serbia, chief of the military academy, from which I retired early in 2002, which was the end of my career. The garrisons in which I served were Nis, Urosevac, Leskovac, Vranje, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Which position did you occupy during the war in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: During the war in Kosovo, or rather, in 1994, I was transferred from Nis to Urosevac [Realtime transcript read in error "Orahovac"] garrison where I was appointed commander of the 243rd Armoured Brigade and, at the same time, garrison commander. My zone of responsibility covered several municipalities in Kosovo and Metohija; namely, Urosevac, Strpce, Stimlje, Kacanik, and part of Vitina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, I have to note that the transcript should say "Urosevac" instead of "Orahovac." Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in the documents, or rather, the exhibits that we have here under tab 1, there is a map. Could you please place it on the easel -- or rather, may I ask the usher to do that, for you to show us your zone of responsibility. It's tab 1. While the usher is placing the map on the easel, could you tell us what you did in Kosovo until 1999, prior to '99.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Prior to 1999, the army performed three basic tasks in Kosovo. They carried out combat training, secured the state border, and ensured the possibility of communication roads in its zone of responsibility. Incidentally, Urosevac is a garrison that has existed from the First World War onwards, and batches of troops were received by the garrison twice a year to go through regular training. In addition to that, we secured a length of the state border facing Macedonia, of 88 kilometres. The border was secured in a line and in depth. We also ensured access to certain intersections and roads; Stimlje, which is the intersection of the road from Lipjan, Kacanik, which forks off to Vitina, Macedonia and Strpce, and further on to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, since the map has been placed on the easel, could you please show us your area of responsibility. And, first of all, tell us what kind of map this is.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from the decision of the Pristina Corps commander, and we have it here in front of us. It was made on the eve of the aggression. The area of responsibility was designated by the corps commander, and it was designated by the superior command, actually. Here we see the Deligrad river -- correction, Debeldelska river, Mala Reka, and further on. That's the border here. Here we see the border with Macedonia, 88 kilometres long. On the west, the border is Prevalac, Sar Planina, Dulje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak about the border, you mean the boundary of your area of responsibility. We see the area of your brigade, which is the 243rd Brigade, and on the east --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: On the east, my neighbour is the 175th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This piece of information will be of assistance for further questions. Could you show us some places on this map that are in your zone of responsibility. In paragraph 63, let me inform you, various allegations are contained concerning our forces. For instance, in 63(j), (k), with subparagraphs under (k), there are references to many places, and I will ask you to explain which of those places are located in your zone of responsibility. I will mention only those that I think were in your zone of responsibility. And if they indeed are, I will ask you to show them on the map and explain at the same time whether those places were also in the combat disposition of your brigade. So in 63(j), we see references to Biba village, Muhadzer Prelez village, Raka village, and Staro Selo.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you about events later. Just show us. Papaz, Sojevo, Mirosavlje, Varos Selo. Tell me, in the combat disposition of your brigade, were these villages located: Biba, Muhadzer Prelez? Can you show us?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were in my area, in the zone of responsibility of my brigade. You enumerated villages that are namely to the east, north, and south of Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show them? I will read out again, so you don't have to memorise them: Biba, Muhadzer Prelez, Raka, Staro Selo, Papaz, Varos Selo, Mirosavlje. All of them are therefore within the combat disposition of your brigade. Further on, in Kacanik municipality, we see references to Kotlina and Ivaja. Can you show them on the map.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then a mention is made of Stagovo village, Slatina, Vata, Dubrava, and lists villages in Kacanik municipality.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the villages that I have read out from this paragraph, paragraph 63 of the indictment, under (j) and (k), are located in the area of responsibility of your brigade and the combat disposition of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. My brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, a moment ago, General, you said what the tasks were in Kosovo and Metohija up until 1999. You told us that. I don't want to go back, but just 1998 and 1999, what did we have in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: In 1998, we have a characteristic situation for the area of my responsibility linked to the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija and it is this: At the beginning of February, individual terrorist groups started to appear. They were groups of three to five members, organised in some way, and they appeared first in a part of Metohija. And with an exchange of information between the units and the superior command, we received information about those groups, and reports about them. One month later, that is to say at the end of February, or rather the first half of March, they appeared in Kosovo, that is to say the area of responsibility of my own brigade. Now, these groups, first and foremost, endeavoured to control part of the communication lines, the roads. They looted on the roads, they would stop people going that way, regardless of their ethnicity, and rob them of their possessions. Money first and even cars. They would confiscate their cars. We have a characteristic example of a bus going from Prizren to Bulgaria and Turkey, taking tourists to a shopping expedition, and they were stopped at Crnoljevo and looted. And in the bus there were mostly Albanians and Turks going that way. These groups, most probably encouraged by their looting and the success they had had in those initial stages, and they were in fact criminals to begin with, they encouraged other groups elsewhere, so that we would have -- see more and more frequent attacks on communication lines and roads, especially those linking Kosovo and Metohija, which means from Stimlje via Suva Reka towards Prizren, and from Urosevac along the roads running to Globocica and Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I can see that you're explaining that to us looking at a map in front of you, but I would like to ask you to point these places out to us on the map behind you. It's the same map but this will enable others to see what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: The communication from Stimlje via Dulje, towards Prizren, and the other road from Urosevac running to Djeneral Jankovic or, rather, Globocica. Those were the main supply lines, supply routes, and main roads leading through southern Kosovo. Those groups were in the mountainous terrains, the forest regions which were fairly inaccessible to the law and order organs, or the MUP. The forces of the MUP undertook measures straight away to protect the population. There were mutual clashes or fighting. And already in the first half of 1998, in the Urosevac MUP, there were more than 20 wounded policemen and several killed policemen. The army of Yugoslavia, or rather, command of the Pristina Corps, in order to protect its own units and to ensure passage along these communication lines, which was one of the roles of the army, issued an order that the units should take up their positions in set locations in order to control the roads and communication routes. One of those units from my own brigade was stationed in the area of Dulje. And its task was to control the road from Stimlje to Suva Reka, to ensure the passage of military vehicles and control over that communication line, to ensure transport. The second group was south of Urosevac in the Doganovic area, and it provided security for the Kacanik communication lines, or the roads running towards Djeneral Jankovic or another road running towards Globocica. Now, with this kind of disposition of troops, we enabled the movement of our own forces, that is to say just the army of Yugoslavia. The MUP worked alongside us to ensure free passage for citizens, vehicles, and to the left and right flanks, ensuring the communication routes I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in tab 2, there's an Official Note which relates to the circumstances of the wounding of six soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia, when the Siptar terrorists attacked military vehicles on the Pristina-Prizren road. And that happened in mid-1998 around the village of Crnoljevo. What can you tell us about this note, this Official Note?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I would just like to say where this document comes from, the origins of it. We said that this communication route was important for our livelihood and our supply routes because communication went from Pristina to Pec and that had already been cut off. The Siptars had control of 40 per cent of the main communication lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This took place in mid-1998. Why don't you bring the witness to events much closer to the essential matters in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just took this document to provide some basic information. General Krsman Jelic -- I wanted General Jelic to tell us how terrorism escalated in Kosovo and Metohija, and this is a document that describes and addresses that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have had an abundance of evidence on the period leading up to 1999, Mr. Milosevic. So let us move on directly to the events in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will come to that, Mr. Robinson. But before we do so, I'd like to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've heard enough about 1998. We've wasted enough time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all I'm asking is that this document be tendered into evidence, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've had an opportunity to look through the 1998 documents. They're plainly relevant military documents showing the state of the situation that the government had to face in 1998. May we suggest that the 1998 documents be admitted into evidence as a collective upon the matters to which they speak, very much in the same terms that the Prosecution used documents during the presentation of their evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll consider that. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure how many '98 documents there are. I don't accept that we put in documents in this way collectively. We've had that discussion before. In fact, there aren't, I think, examples of this kind of document going in collectively. I accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think there are more than seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I accept that, of course, '98 has relevance. The Chamber will remember the degree to which Lord Ashdown's evidence from both May and September of 1998 is being challenged, and of course the Prosecution's case is that there had already been a descent into illegal criminality by that stage known to the accused and those engaged with them. So I don't challenge the broad acceptability -- the admissibility of some '98 material. How it should be dealt with is a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to come back on that, C-37, the first Croatian witness the Prosecution called, produced a large number of documents that had been provided to him concerning the TO in a particular area of western -- of Croatia, and those were documents relating to the activities and organisation of the local TO that had been found by the Croatian MUP, given to the Prosecution, and put in as a collective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to assist the Court, because I made a particular assertion, and to back it up, it's Exhibit 334, Croatian police files, a whole collective that the witness C-37 put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will admit these documents, the seven documents up to tab 7, as a collection. Let a number be given to the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D329, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: D329, yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying this: That's all fine, but I would like to raise certain questions with respect to some documents, to ask questions about them, because if something is being ordered in 1998 with respect to conduct towards the enemy side, that is an order of the Supreme Command which isn't extinguished at that point. It applies to the ensuing period. So you have to see what is being ordered and what it applies to. So if we're talking about an event, such as the one in tab 2, I completely agree; we don't have to go through it at all. However, in tab 3, for example, we have a corps commander order, and the advantage of it is that it was given in 1998 and not post festum, at some other time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, I think you have a point. So tab 3, you want to ask something in relation to tab 3. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please, you have tab 3 in front of you. It's an order which you received; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The order comes from your immediate superior command, that is to say, the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell us, what about the operations carried out against Siptar terrorist forces? What was ordered? Especially pursuant to this order. Look at point 1. Order, and then point 1.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Point 1 regulates this. It says: "... during operations against Siptar terrorists, very rational use of combat equipment should be used. Combat equipment should be used solely to neutralise well-fortified firing positions of the Siptar terrorists and group targets, taking care not to damage residential buildings."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's what point 1 of the order says. What about point 2? It says that something is prohibited.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says: "Prohibit causing damage to facilities in settlements from which Siptar terrorists have been expelled, regardless of whether they stayed in them earlier and put up resistance from them," armed resistance from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean, then? You are told to fire at a facility only if there is resistance coming from there. That is to say, there is -- it is prohibited to cause damage on any of the facilities.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It says particularly forbid torching of houses and other auxiliary buildings. And then once again --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In point 3, it says: "I again warn ..." which means that there was a caution issued previously.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the orders we received. "I again warn unit commanders -" brigade commanders - "and prohibit the taking of personal property from abandoned houses, and from citizens, as was the case..." in certain units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says: "I again warn unit commanders and prohibit the taking of personal property -" which means "from abandoned houses," which means that even if a house is abandoned, they are not allowed to touch any property. And it goes on to say: "... as was the case in the 125th Motorised Brigade, the 549th Motorised Brigade," et cetera. And then he goes on to say that: "All goods misappropriated so far will be returned to the place where they were taken from." And a deadline is given. "Goods are to be returned by August the 9th, 1998 ..." and that disciplinary and criminal measures should be taken against individuals who have disobeyed orders. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says: "Disciplinary and criminal measures will be taken against individuals who have disobeyed orders ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end, it says that all the members of the unit should be informed of this: "... inform all members of the units about this Order." So that was your duty, to inform each and every soldier; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, the soldiers and the combat groups as well; that is to say, the groups that are already on the field. To the very last soldier, they must all be aware of that and made aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I assume that I don't have to ask you about this document now because you said that it will be admitted into evidence, and that we needn't go through them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like either Mr. Kay or Mr. Nice to check whether this is an identical exhibit with D300, 104. If yes, this is simply a waste of time. Please proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document that General Krsman Jelic got. It can be seen on the document. You can see the stamp of his brigade there, the command of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. He received it on the 7th of August, 1998. So it's his document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think General Delic has got the same order from General Pavkovic. Go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite certain, Mr. Kwon, that all brigade commanders will get the same orders from the corps. However, now we have a document where it says 243rd Brigade, and that is why it differs from the document received from Dr. -- from Pavkovic, or rather, it supports that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in tab 4, there is an order from the Pristina Corps. That's already September 1998. What can be seen in this first paragraph? It says: "The situation in Kosovo and Metohija ... has become increasingly complex in recent days owing to constant pressure by Siptar terrorists on the civilian population, preventing them from returning to populated areas. For this reason, a large number of civilians remain in the woods." Was that the situation?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you could personally perceive?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct; that a great portion of the population had left their homes because of the activities of the Siptar terrorists. And because of assessments made in the field, the corps commander is stating all of this; namely, that they were using the civilian population for protection and for preventing them from leaving the combat zone in good time. They change their clothing and they leave the area together with the civilian population, or, under their protection, surrender to MUP. "The foreign media and some journalists are putting forward a theory about a so-called humanitarian catastrophe for the Siptar population, and are attempting to get world public opinion to put pressure on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its leadership to halt MUP operations against terrorist strongholds, and thereby allegedly prevent the 'humanitarian catastrophe.' "The Yugoslav Government, MUP units, and the VJ are attempting to offer all necessary assistance to the refugee population and return them to their homes, and in some villages, the population has largely returned to their homes with the assistance of the MUP and the VJ forces." Given the above, the corps commander ordered that: "All commands will undertake measures to prevent the use of hardware in sectors where there is a civilian population until they have left and are being cared for, and additionally continue with all measures previously ordered by the Pristina Corps command. "When breaking up diversionary terrorist forces, undertake all measures to discover in good time sectors where the civilian population is grouping and leaving, and ensure that they are directed to and received in secure sectors, and when the DTS have been broken up, their organised return to the populated areas."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Food and health care should be provided. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Also, in paragraph 5, it says: "All commands will undertake measures and issue orders to govern relations with the civilian population and their property, and prevent its being stolen. In the event of violation of orders, undertake measures against all violators, and immediately report about this to the superior command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, is this document already an exhibit in the trial?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I don't know, because General Delic had set documents too, as far as the corps is concerned. But this is the link with the order of General Krsman Jelic, which follows in tab 5, and that certainly was not tendered before. It was not admitted before, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where the document is already an exhibit, what's the point in having this witness spend time reading through it? He gets exactly the same communication as General Delic. This is not only a waste of time, it's an abuse of the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Go directly to tab 5. Tab 4 looks to me to be identical with tab 136 of D300.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What have we got here in tab 5, General? Is this an order that you signed?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my document, my order, which pertains to the prohibition of the use of combat equipment. It's an order. I wrote this to the commands of Combat Group 1 and Combat Group 2 and the military police battalion that was subordinated to me. And it says here: "In view of the prevailing complex political and security situation, the constant presence of UN --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to quote all of it. But you say here in paragraph 2, at the beginning: "Pursuant to the strictly confidential order of the Pristina Corps ..." et cetera, the number doesn't matter --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "... of October 3rd, 1998, and in order to implement consistently the decisions of the President of the Republic of Serbia and the President of the FRY on the withdrawal of troops to barracks, I hereby issue the following: Order ..." So the units are withdrawing to barracks.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what do you say?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I say: "Order: I most strictly forbid to use combat equipment (tanks, self-propelled and artillery guns), except in the event of a direct attack on military installations and troop deployment sectors. "2. Thoroughly investigate each breach of this order and the circumstances leading to the use of the above-mentioned weapons and take the violators to account."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could I please have an explanation now. According to this order, the order that applied to the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the troops were withdrawn into barracks, and according to the same agreement, a few combat groups were left where?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: In the area of Kosovo and Metohija, three combat groups were left: Lapusnik, Volujak and Dulje. From my brigade, the combat group was in Dulje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the combat group that was in that area, in accordance with this agreement, when the army withdrew into the barracks. So in 1998 and 1999, they were there all the time.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: They were there until the 15th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Its presence was specifically established, agreed upon, with the OSCE; right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, and approved, as well as its size. The basic task was, as I already mentioned, to protect roads and to escort military convoys from Stimlje to Dulje, or rather via Dulje to Suva Reka and further on to Prizren. So to secure that road, because from the 14th of June all the way to the end of July, that road had been cut off, a month and a half, due to the activity of the Siptar terrorist forces. In order to prevent that from happening in the future, the combat group remained there and that was its basic task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. So throughout this time, in 1998 and 1999, until the beginning of the war - not to discuss the time after that - was its composition stable in terms of size, the strength of that unit? What did it consist of? And show us exactly where it was located.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: This combat group was located --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This combat group Dulje, what did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: All three combat groups were the strength of a company respectively; about 150 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was fixed; right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Its establishment was fixed in terms of size, the number of personnel, and the quantity of combat equipment. The number of APCs, the number of tanks, that was strictly set. However, its locality was not strictly fixed. It was based in Dulje, but its task was to be on the move, providing security for vehicles that were moving along that road, Crnoljevo, Dulje, Suva Reka and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that the members of that combat group met convoys, escorted them through the gorge, and returned.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That combat group had two subgroups. One was in Stimlje, where it was based, and where it met vehicles, announced and unannounced vehicles. And then if these were motor vehicles, then they escorted them with their own wheel-propelled vehicles, Pragas and BRDMs primarily. But if they were combat units, then of course we had training, like other units. Then they used combat vehicles and then we used heavy equipment, combat vehicles to escort these columns. There was a subgroup in Stimlje and there was a subgroup south of Dulje, about 2 kilometres south, in the area of Birac, between Dulje and Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, while we are still dealing with that map, I omitted to ask for this map to be tendered, and that is tab 1. What is the date of this map?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: March 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is a contemporaneous map pertaining to your area of responsibility and the combat disposition of your forces.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Exactly. That is an excerpt from the order of the commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I omitted to ask for tab 1, this map, to be admitted into evidence. That's how we started the examination today, and Jelic indicated all these different places that I mentioned on the basis of that map, so could it please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 6, there is an order of the chief of staff of the Pristina Corps which pertains to what? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: This is an order dating back to October. Some units were using certain facilities. The commander of the Pristina Corps, or rather, the chief of staff here, prohibits the use of privately owned buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what he orders. And in tab 7, we have your order.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does your order say? Let's not waste time with the corps command order.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: On the basis of their order, I issued an order too to my groups that are in the actual area; to the 1st Mechanised Battalion that was in Dulje, and the 3rd Battalion of the military police. Paragraph 1: "Immediately leave privately-owned furnished houses, if any are being used."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they are being used, then they should be left; right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 2: "Leave all private items found in the houses in them. I forbid their removal." Paragraph 3: "Assign units to accommodation in socially-owned facilities. Private facilities which are not furnished may also be used if necessary." And then I make it incumbent upon the commanders of the 1st and 3rd Battalions to be directly responsible to me for carrying out this order. I must say that my units in Dulje and the battalion of the military police were in socially-owned and military facilities. Actually, in Dulje, we already had a half-built building, and the 1st Battalion was there, stationed at Dulje, and the 3rd Battalion was in a socially-owned factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. So we've briefly dealt with these documents that pertain to 1998. General, tell us now, as we're getting closer to 1999 in your testimony, at the end of this 1998, what was your knowledge concerning the KLA? What kind of information did the army have? What was the nature of their organisation, their units? Tell us in the briefest possible terms about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I've already said what their organisation was: Until June, groups of three to five, possibly ten men, that were primarily engaged in criminal activity; looting, rape, abduction, killing. In the second half of 1998, their numbers increased. Unfortunately, increasing quantities of weapons were brought in from Albania and partly from Macedonia. Only at our border crossings, until the month of June, we seized about 70 automatic rifles, most of them Chinese-made; about 90-something pistols; tens of thousands of pieces of ammunition, different calibres; a few kilogrammes of narcotic drugs; a large quantity of medical supplies; and over 50 tonnes of different commodities that were smuggled primarily from western Macedonia into Kosovo and Metohija. This was a sign and an indicator that these groups will be even better armed, better organised. We had information from our superior command, from units on the ground, from the state security, the MUP, and it was realised that these groups were being established primarily by way of village staffs whose sizes differed, depending on the size of the village concerned and its layout. This particularly pertained to hilly and mountainous areas where their brigades were established. In my area of responsibility was the operative zone Nerodimlje, as they called it. There were three brigades: The 161st, which was to the south of Stimlje, in these villages: Rance, Vranje, Racak, Malopoljce, in those villages. The 162nd Brigade was in the area of Kacanik, and it was between these roads, from Kacanik to Djeneral Jankovic and from Kacanik to Globocica. The 163rd Brigade was partly mobilised and was in the western part of Vitina. Those brigades had a total of 1.000 to 1.500 men. Their activity was a continuation of the activity of those groups. And they stepped up their efforts after the verifiers arrived and after the army withdrew into the barracks. And this was in the area that we held until we withdrew into the barracks, and that is precisely the area that these units of theirs took up then. Their activities targeted mainly the state authorities, the army, and the police. In view of the fact that the greatest part of the population there are ethnic Albanians, they pressured even Albanians, mobilising people by force. One of the ways in which they did it was to call up these people and distribute weapons to them. We had information that several hundred people had been killed or abducted, mainly Albanians who had failed to respond to their call-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a sufficiently long narrative. Time to ask a question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you showed us a moment ago the location of your combat group pursuant to the agreement, the one that you said was one company strong, conditionally called Dulje Combat Group. You have a different name for it, but that's the one I mean. You told us in which locations it was, beginning with October 1998 onwards, although you said it was there even before October 1998. How far was it from Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: The command of the combat group was about 15 kilometres away from Racak. One of its subgroups was in Birac, south of Dulje, 2 or 3 kilometres south of Dulje, whereas another subgroup was in the area of Stimlje, Canovica Hill, namely. That is very close to Stimlje, about 500 metres away, along the Stimlje-Trnjevo-Dulje road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far from Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies, 1 kilometre, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since it was in the area of responsibility of your brigade, apart from the stationary group in that location, were there any other army groups, units, in that location around Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, but I want to explain this in particular. Temporarily the number of people in that combat group could lower occasionally, because some of its troops were seconded to escort transports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it never increased?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, because we always complied with the agreement, and the number of troops and combat equipment had to be fixed at a certain level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have a number of allegations here in the indictment, namely, paragraph 63(a) -- 66(a), rather, that refers to events in Racak, municipality of Stimlje. What can you tell us about this, General? Because the only unit in the vicinity was your unit. What can you tell us about the events in Racak on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of January, the chief of SUP, Bogoljub Janicevic, who testified here before me, informed me of what had happened to their forces that controlled the traffic between Urosevac and Stimlje. He said that several days previously three of their policemen had been killed. MUP forces constantly worked to find the perpetrators, and through their sources and associates and the State Security Service, they got hold of information that in the broad area of Racak, namely, the Jezerske mountains and around Racak and around Malopoljce there was a strong terrorist group, part of one of those brigades that I mentioned. On the 14th, the chief of MUP called me into his office and informed me of the plan that they had established, along with the information they had gathered on the enemy. He also told me that they had received approval to go forward with the previously prepared plan to crush that terrorist group. The point of inviting me for this talk was to inform me that, in my close vicinity, there was a unit of the MUP, just 500 metres away, and the road and part of my forces were in the area, my troops, one of my units. He said that they would start the action in the early morning hours. The next day, early morning, I think it was around 3 a.m., they started putting up the blockade, and around 7 a.m., the blockade was complete and the search for terrorists started. From the time when the first shots were fired, when fighting began around 8 a.m., fire was opened on part of my brigade, or rather, combat group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you, General, to look at this. We can put it on the ELMO because it's not a big map. But it is a very large-scale map; 1:12.500. Is that the same one that I have? It's the map of Racak, 1:12.500. What can you see at the top?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That is the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Leave it on the ELMO, please, and you will explain. General, before we take a look at the map - I placed it there so you can explain the events - but before that, you brought a document that was issued on the 9th of January, 1999. It's in tab 8. It's an order issued by you, and it's a good idea to keep in mind the preceding documents. So this document is dated the 9th of January, 1999, some six days before Racak.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Right. This is my document, and that is the correct date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your signature, your order. What does it refer to? "Monitor the activities --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have a reference, please, for this quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We need a reference, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 8, I said, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Point 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 8, point 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Second page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have it. Point 5 at tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what does this order refer to, in the briefest possible terms?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Maintenance and stepping up of the combat-readiness of units. I constantly issued orders, at least one per month, to maintain a high level of combat-readiness in view of the environment, in view of our tasks, and in view of the tasks that we would be given in the future. You said that one of these points is to "Monitor activities of the forces engaged in guarding the state border and in the area, and in controlling the sectors and axes in the zone of responsibility; thwart any movement or activities by Siptar terrorists." Part of our unit was, indeed, engaged in guarding the state border in depth, assisting the border units that were stationed along the line of the state border. We had to maintain high levels of combat-readiness because we had intervention units within our troops that needed to be combat-ready at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was your obligation to be very alert in your monitoring of the conduct and possible activities of sabotage terrorist forces and respond accordingly.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To secure the state border in depth and to maintain high combat-readiness of combat groups, like the one in Dulje. And that applies to all units of the brigade that had some sort of mission.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: All units of the brigade that were in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 11th of January, there is another order issued by you, referring to what?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Security to be provided of the state border. That border used to be very porous and had to be completely sealed, outside border crossings, of course. That's why this order was written, to raise the level of combat-readiness even higher in view of the engagement -- further engagement of units in the planning, application, and constant upgrading of tactics, monitoring of organs, strengthening the responsibility of all concerned, preventing unusual incidents and other forms of threats. Further on: "Upgrade the systems of intelligence, security, engineering, logistic and other support to the units," because without good support, we would be unable to perform our tasks. Then to raise the level of combat-readiness and in-depth security of the state border, to improve the coordination and coordinated action of all within the security system, and so on. I set myself the task, in paragraph 2, to continue to treat the security of the state border as the brigade's priority task, and to make sure that combat group commanders and all unit commanders devote two-thirds of their time to security tasks. To organise groups with real needs in providing security to the state border, to tailor the missions and assignments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've had enough now, Mr. Milosevic, about combat-readiness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 10, we see your order that deals with upgrading and maintenance, dated the 15th of January, 1999. It refers again to planned and organised preparations to detect enemy activities and criminal activities, enhancing the performance of units in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, may I tender tabs 8, 9, and 10, because they concern activities at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This set of orders, does it also include tab 11?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you going to come back to Racak, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I will. I just wanted to take it in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this set of orders dealing with securing the state border, does it include the tab 11 order?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of our obligations was also to put up obstacles in the state border belt, with a view to securing the state border. I ordered to continue laying obstacles in the border area along the critical axes as designated. Because the border can never be physically sealed, obstacles were necessary. "2. Setting up barrier systems ... by laying groups of mines and minefields. "3. Obstacles along characteristic axes (valleys, gorges, streams and so on) are to be laid by constructing and laying down anti-tank barriers, anti-tank obstacles, Brun spirals and wire fences ..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we now come back, in order to follow the chronology, to Racak and your knowledge about the events in Racak. You already told us that the MUP chief informed you he was planning an action in the vicinity of one of your units.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where exactly was that unit of yours? To determine exactly how close it was to the planned area of activity, could you show us on the map? First on one map and then on a more detailed map.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Part of the combat group was -- here is Stimlje. Do you see the road from Stimlje to Dulje, rather, Stimlje-Crnoljevo-Dulje. I guess it's, from Stimlje there is the Borovo wood towards Canovica Hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, show the same thing on a more detailed map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: So this is the little town of Stimlje, the road going through to the Crnoljevo gorge, towards Dulje and further on to Prizren. Canovica Hill, elevation 671, to the south of it is a forest, a fir forest, and part of the combat group was inside the forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a pen, or whatever is handy, to mark the location of that part of your combat group.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: You see this road --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just make a little circle.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. To the right of the road, in this fir forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was this the only unit that was located close to Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That was the only combat unit, part of the combat group. That was its only location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was its composition?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Its composition was as follows: It had three tanks, three APCs, three Pragas, and three BRDMs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means 12 vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: About 12 vehicles, although this changed. If some vehicles went off towards the column, then there were less; or coming from Dulje, there would be two or three more vehicles. But the overall combat group, with this composition at Dulje - and this is the subgroup - did not change in size.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How far was your unit from Racak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Racak, well, about 1 kilometre as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we take a look at the overhead projector, please, and have you focus on Racak. Oh, we see Racak now on the screens. So the combat group is below Canovica Hill, and Racak is over here. Tell us now, please, General, that unit, the one you marked using your pen, it was there since Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: This unit, pursuant to agreement with the verifiers, was there from October. Otherwise, it came out in April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from April 1998, that unit was there in order to provide security for this communication line; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described to us its composition, who made it up, and you were informed by Janicevic that they had an operation in Racak because you were right close by.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you agree with him, or did he ask you to take part in this action in Racak at all?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, no, because I wasn't there pursuant to a plan, and you cannot deploy the army unless you have an order or plan. You have written traces of a command and you have to have the decision made by the superior command if we were to take part in any operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But did he ask you to support him, give him reinforcement if the need arose?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, he did not ask for reinforcements, and he didn't need to, because he said he had enough men to deal with the situation, since there was a group over there whom they thought was a terrorist group and had attacked three policemen going from Stimlje to Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, on that day, did you intervene at all in any way? Did you have occasion to intervene at Racak at all?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, at no point, and there was no need for that. We were not asked to send reinforcements and to help out, so that intervention was impossible, even had we wished to do so, if there were people there who were searching the terrain in order to capture the terrorists --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just bear this in mind: The other side is claiming here that the army took part, together with the police, in the events in Racak, and that this is -- and that there is an attempt to cover this up. Now, as that was the only combat group, the one you described and the one you marked on the map that was there pursuant to agreement with the OSCE, did the army in any way have any action to do with Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No. Literally no. Not on the previous days, not on that day, not later on afterwards. There was no action vis-a-vis Racak ever since April. There was only one incident when the combat operation started and when there was shooting, above the village of Belince, which is about 800 metres away from Racak, or 3 or 400 metres away. From this forest region, there was shooting coming at this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us better.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: It was this area here, according to reconnaissance work carried out by the soldiers. They opened fire from an anti-aircraft machine-gun -- yes, anti-aircraft machine-gun. We were fired at, and two to three mortar shells were fired at us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, at us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not from Racak.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, not from Racak, from the area south of Belince. And we responded to that fire with a sporadic round of gunfire. We waited for 15, 20 minutes to see whether there was any movement. If there was, and there was, we opened fire from Praga and the machine-gun, and then it was silence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only point in time, the only occasion when that combat group of yours shot was in response to firing coming at it from the village of Belince, or rather, south of the village of Belince; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there wasn't any shooting at Racak; Racak wasn't targeted at all.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No. And you can't even see Racak from that area there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you indicate that for us on the map. Show that on the map.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: It was feature 637. 637, you can see it here. And this area is higher -- at a higher altitude than where the unit is. After they opened fire, it took up its positions in the defence region. The tanks were here, and there's a report that I sent to the corps command, the Howitzers had already been positioned there, but they can't shoot at a short distance. It's less than 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you want to say, what you're telling us is that not even theoretically were you able to open fire at Racak even if you wanted to do so.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: From our positions, no, we could not. All we could do was to enter Racak. That's all we could have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that was a leading question --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was. It leads us to the break

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before we have the break, can I ask you one thing, General: What was the date on which your troops were fired upon? Are you saying this was on the 15th of January, or is this on some other occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was the 15th of January, between 8 and 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you were asked by the accused to briefly describe what happened in Racak, you said like this: "The next day -" which is the 15th - "in early morning, I think it was around 3 a.m., they started putting up the blockade, and around 7 a.m. the blockade was complete and the search for terrorists started. From the time when the first shots were fired, when fighting began around 8 a.m., fire was opened on part of my brigade, or rather, combat group." Did you mean at that time that the firing against -- to the direction of Belince, not to Racak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fire that was opened between the village of Belince and the village of Racak, but closer to the village of Belince.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What confuses me is you've marked a point on the map at point 637, and that was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- not the position of the firing, that's simply the high point on the ground, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's an elevation separating -- a slope separating this area. The road is lower, then you have a valley, and then you have fir trees and the forest starting that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yours was the only unit, army unit, in the Racak area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Of the Yugoslav army, that was the only unit, one single unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll take the break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just to clarify certain points, Mr. Bonomy asked you why you had marked this feature 637 -- 697, which was opposite your positions. For me not to ask leading questions, you explained the topography of the area. So why did you mark that particular spot?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: It is feature 637.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: It's a slope which runs parallel to the road and from which point you cannot see the village of Racak, except perhaps the south or south-western reaches of the village. So from this area here, you cannot see Racak. And bearing in mind that the road is lower than this elevation and that this land is lower lying, you cannot see the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You showed us that feature. Why? To show that between your positions and the village of Racak is a hill? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you said it was a leading question, but I was just trying to clarify what the witness had already stated, which was that between the position of his unit and the village of Racak, you have this hill here, this elevation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Then let him give the evidence. Let him give that evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you enumerated the type of weapons and pieces that this unit had, artillery weapons that the unit had in this area here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any artillery that this unit had that could have targeted Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Heavy weapons? No. You couldn't target it from this area, when there was an emergency proclaimed and when they opened fire. All it could do was this broader section of the road here. This was a road where columns from Pristina or Urosevac or Gnjilani were met and escorted. You could open fire only on a part of the territory towards Belince and towards Vrana, which is this angle here, a 20-degree angle, 15- to 20-degree angle here. Otherwise, you can't see Belince proper, but just the outlying houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that on the basis of this topographical map. You can see the difference in altitude. So the only time fire was opened on that day, as you have explained to us, was in response to the shooting, the fire coming from your -- rather, in response to fire coming at your unit from the hill which is 781, feature 781.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: South of Belince.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, south of Belince. So that's the only time fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were several bursts of gunfire until they stopped shooting at our positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, tell me this: Your unit that day, did it move at all?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: From the area, except to take up its defence positions, which is what every army does when it's being shot at, there was no other movement. It didn't move out of the area at all. And this patrol stayed there throughout, in the next few days and all the time, where this road widens, that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does "this patrol" mean a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In fact, it's a checkpoint. It's a patrol controlling the incoming vehicles and to see whether they were military vehicles, their legitimate passage, and escorting them or providing security through the ravine, which is about 15 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was there a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was there a tank at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that period, or rather, usually fast vehicles are kept there, because they are to escort motor vehicles. A tank cannot do that; it's too slow. That's its technical feature, and also the features of the communications route. So the BRDMs, mostly, those vehicles, and the Praga vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you mean to say that the firing at your combat group came from the feature 781, which is what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the forest here with no name. That's where they opened fire at positions of my unit, or the combat group in the area, from artillery pieces and mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now generally, in the course of the day, from that position of yours, did you open fire on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Except for responding to the shooting at us, on that day and the following day, we did not open fire, and we did not open fire the previous day either. So we did not open fire from this position here. There was no need to do so either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on that day, the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Well, I was in the brigade headquarters, the command there, and I was commanding my unit, the Urosevac area -- Urosevac garrison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we now take a look -- let me just take a moment to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll admit this map as marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If you're going to admit it, that's a very good thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, would you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's have a number for that, Mr. Milosevic, before you proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D330, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I was saying, the circle or the mark that you made to signify your unit's position, it's the oval there, or whatever, so you can write the unit's position up there. It denotes the position of the unit.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now an arrow.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what you have just marked, or rather, what you marked in there where your marker pen is now, that's the area from which your unit was fired at. So that means, if you write that down, the region that the shooting came from and to which you responded with your fire power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I could ask the General also to mark the position of the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you have marked in as 637, that is the hill between your positions and the village of Racak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, write that down, then. "Hill between your positions and the village of Racak."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Jelic, can I ask how you came to know all about this. You said you were in Urosevac. How were you informed of this happening, firing at Belince and firing from Belince? How did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's very simple in the army: The system of command and reporting is clearly defined. The commander of the combat group, as soon as they -- as soon as fire was opened, he took measures to protect his equipment and men; that's the first thing he did. And the second thing he did was to report back to me. So reporting was the basic means of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you received a report in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, by telephone. By telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who was it that reported to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commander of Combat Group 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is Colonel Djordjevic, who was then a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like to put a few questions to you in connection with a document that was here before. It was presented by the other side. Since I want to deal with it briefly, I've made a sufficient number of copies for all who are here. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please take this. This is a record of a meeting, or rather a visit to the 243rd Brigade, written by General Maisonneuve, or rather, one of his people, one of his co-workers. First comes his original English text, and then you have a translation into the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got this in front of you, General?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think any of the Court is using the file of Racak materials, but this, of course, is one of those, and it's tab 9 in it if you're looking for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are going to get to that now, but first I have a few questions for you. General Maisonneuve was one of the members of the verification mission. He was heard here as a witness. And he stated that after the incident in Racak, the commander of the brigade in Urosevac, that is to say you, did not want to see him; that he managed to see you only three weeks later when he succeeded in convincing Colonel Kotur that he should persuade you to have that meeting. That is what he said in May 2002. The transcript page is 5871. Are these statements correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, I was not there. I was absent. I was away on official business. Mr. Maisonneuve came on that day. I could not see him; I could not see him. The next scheduled meeting, or rather he did not schedule that meeting -- I mean, anyway, I had been absent then, so it was not that I was supposed to be there. As for the next meeting, I was out in the field, and for objective reasons, he was told that I could not arrive on time. So then he scheduled a meeting for the following day, and I did attend that meeting, which is to say that when he scheduled the meeting, except for that one day before that I was not there because I was down there near Dulje, towards Javor, touring my units. And when somebody schedules a meeting within the course of one hour, of course you cannot arrive in time, especially not in the winter, January, snow. These are the slopes of Mount Sara. You'll see that the altitude goes all the way up to 1.000 metres, and snow can be one metre deep at that time. So he was told that I could not come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he stated -- and, gentlemen, for you, that is transcript page 5790 -- that he first made Kotur talk you into seeing him, and that at the meeting with you, you did not want to confirm that you cooperated with the MUP during the operation of Racak, as they call it, and that you were not firing at that village but that you were firing at two other villages. That's what his report says. And you did not want to confirm that the military and the MUP acted together in Racak.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I cannot just confirm something that somebody wishes to here if that was not the case. I can only confirm facts. The army did not participate. And what I'm confirming is that it did not participate, because that is a fact. He probably expected me to say something, but there was no reason for that to happen. When the military did take part in something, when there were joint coordinated plans, we never avoided saying so. We always have to say the truth and we have to present proper arguments. But the army did not take part here, it did not have a plan, it did not have orders, and therefore it could not have been used either. You know that the army can be used in combat only if it is directly attacked, if its safety and security is jeopardised. It is only then that it can respond with fire. As for Mr. Kotur, he could not persuade me and he could not issue orders to me. He was the deputy head of the Verification Mission between our Pristina Corps and the verifiers. He did not have the right to issue orders. His activity focused on an exchange of experience with them and submitting things that the military wanted to have said.
