So it went -- everything went through our liaison officers and then through him and then through General Loncar with the verifiers, because there cannot be dual command in the army, there can only be a single command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. He also said here that the patrols of the Verification Mission were on the hills surrounding Racak and that they were observing the operation from there, and that they saw tanks of the army of Yugoslavia that were firing at houses. He even says that in these houses there were people, because you could see smoke coming out of the chimneys.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: If we see the position where he was, tanks did not enter Racak, did not leave the camp. Tank fire can be heard very well, so it's not something that may just seem to be the case. So from this area, from this area where he -- where it was, it could not have fired even theoretically, because a tank can fire only in a straight line from minus 5 to plus 22 degrees, and it cannot fire through a hill that is 5 or 600 metres high, and it cannot fire at a populated area in that way. So the tank did not fire, the army did not fire from a tank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clarify one point in relation to this. After what happened in Racak, Mr. Maisonneuve -- he speaks of this on transcript page 5778, and he says that he came to talk to you and to ask you what happened, and he asked you to confirm that your troops were involved. And he says Colonel Petrovic confirmed that the MUP did take part, carried out an action at Racak, but that it was supported by Pragas and tanks from the brigade, that is to say from the army of Yugoslavia. Can you say something about Mr. Maisonneuve's statement? Did he really say, Colonel Petrovic, did he really say what Maisonneuve said?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic attended this meeting but Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic did not say that. He actually confirmed what I stated a few moments ago; namely, that the army did not go in and did not open fire and there was no need for them to do so and they did not have orders to that effect. Again, opening fire at a long range, I point out once again, when the MUP already entered this built-up area, and you don't know where the line is, and even with the best of intentions, if you wanted to do that, and even if you were to do this of your own free will, arbitrarily, you're not allowed to open fire because our units are already there, or rather, the MUP is already there in the village. So you would not be firing at forces that are fighting against terrorists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, he also stated that he talked to the liaison officer and that he was not pleased not to have been able to talk to you, and that the liaison officer said that Stimlje had been dealt with with Pragas, military vehicles, and a tank, and it was his understanding that this was support from the army of Yugoslavia. Do you know anything about that conversation? Who did Maisonneuve talk to at the time, and is this correct, what he said?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I don't want to sound insulting, but this is a bit senseless, what he says. How can you deal with Stimlje with Pragas and tanks when the authorities are in Stimlje? This is the seat of a municipality. The MUP is there, all the institutions of the municipality. Tanks were not firing at these buildings where the population is, where citizens are. Stimlje, of course, was never in the hands of terrorists. And, after all, the MUP commanded from that area. It commanded their own units that were in Racak, from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure if there's some confusion about the document that's been distributed. I'm a little confused myself, because the accused has been proceeding almost on the basis that the document you've been provided is a record of the conversation with this witness and General Maisonneuve. In fact, the document you've got is the earlier one, which is the record of the conversation with others, including Petrovic, and the record of the conversation with this witness is at tab 28 of the Racak documents, if you want to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you have the relevant document here? Is it, in fact, tab 28? Because what Mr. Nice says is that this witness is not involved in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to deal with this document that I've just handed out to you now, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You want to deal with this document in any event.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means, because it is an important document. And the conversation took place with the liaison officer of General Jelic, because this Colonel Petrovic is from his brigade. He was his commander. It's not important whether he personally took part in the discussion or not, because his own liaison officer participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you probably did suggest that this witness was involved in the conversation, but proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm confused. Do you mean a liaison officer other than Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying is that this is a record of the conversation with Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic, who is the liaison officer of General Jelic's brigade; that is, the brigade that is under General Jelic's command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have this record before you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic inform you about the discussion with General Maisonneuve and his team?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did inform me about the content of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Racak took place on the 15th of January. I assume that there is no need to establish that. That is a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This conversation took place on the 16th of January. That is what it says here in this record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the morning of the 16th of January, at 10.37 local time, this conversation took place. In this record that we see here, these are their notes. "P" is Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that the MUP was -- "Stimlje done by MUP with Praga, AVs, and one tank. Don't know how they were dealing with it." Do you understand this? Do you know what Petrovic was saying? Does this seem truthful to you? I mean I don't know how to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The series of three questions reveal the impossibility of the witness dealing with what's being asked of him in one way or another. If you want to know what Petrovic said, call him. We haven't even heard from the accused through the witness how it is being asserted this witness was informed of the conversation and when. It may be there is a written record. This is the army. Perhaps we should see the record of what Petrovic said to his superior, but it hasn't been produced. But, really, the last question is wholly unacceptable, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't see how this witness can usefully, helpfully, comment on the conversation between General Maisonneuve and Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic. If Colonel Petrovic told him something, then that's a different matter. You may wish to pursue that line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely the line I was about to pursue, Mr. Robinson. The lieutenant colonel was his subordinate and his liaison officer. Maisonneuve --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent that Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic reported anything to him, I think that's a legitimate area of inquiry by you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you were informed or not by Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic about Maisonneuve's visit and the conversation he had with him.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did inform me of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, let's establish whether he informed you exactly, and when that was. Did he say it was on the morning of the 16th, as it says in General Maisonneuve's notes?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the early hours of the morning, at 10.37, as it says here, during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, it says here in this record the meeting started at 1037 hours. And when --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I make the request that the accused tries to deal with it properly. The proper way to deal with it would be to turn the record over and ask a series of non-leading questions to establish what, and on what basis, the witness's recollection is. If we can't do that, any answers that come out are likely to be a complete waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there is merit in that submission. You must try to elicit from the witness what he was told by his subordinate. I think referring to the conversation here is not going to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just ask General Jelic what he had heard from Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness has got the document, by the way, in front of him, and it is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask General Jelic whether Colonel Petrovic kept a record of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure he did. Certainly. He kept records of all his meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did he pass that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents, up until 1998, according to orders from the superior command, all had to be submitted to the commander at the time, the Pristina Corps, with the command and headquarters in Pristina itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, now: Did he hand it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't hand it to me, because the brigade commander doesn't keep the documents. It is the administration that has the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when he reported the meeting to you, he didn't give you a copy of his record. You just got an account by word of mouth from him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He gave me a copy of the record. It was read, it was registered, and handed over to the archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the obvious thing to have done here would have been to bring it along, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received this document here, from the accused, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't bring it in.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. And could the witness's second microphone be switched on, please, as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't suppose we're challenging that this meeting with your liaison officer was on the 16th, in the morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, take a look at page 2 of this record, the one-but-last --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is what I thought he was not to be allowed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, apparently you don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness has got the document over in front of him, so probably all this effort to make the evidence of value will be set at naught. Perhaps the witness could be invited not to look at a document and to cast his mind back, and if the accused can't ask questions, maybe Mr. Kay could be invited to stand up and do the job for him. It's about time it was done properly. We've wasted, I think, 10 minutes or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must ask the witness whether he had a conversation with Brigadier General Maisonneuve; what was the subject of the conversation, did it relate to Racak; questions along that line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, all I want to do is to establish certain material facts. This record, as compiled by Maisonneuve, is a material fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has already ruled that it is not allowing you to utilise the material in this way, so you must get at it by some other means.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did Petrovic inform you about what General Maisonneuve had asked of him on the morning of the 16th of January?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, Lieutenant Colonel, informed me about the contents of the meeting. He handed in a report, it was read, and it was handed over to the archives. The focus of their conversation was on the following: That Colonel Petrovic should confirm that the army had taken part in Racak; that's one point. And secondly, he asked for the names of the commanders for war crimes, at 10.37, at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's what I wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've heard that, Mr. Robinson, you've heard what the witness has said without using the material at hand, and now he can use the material at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We've already ruled. He can tell you what Petrovic told him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, a moment ago the witness said that Petrovic informed him that Maisonneuve had asked him to confirm that the army had taken part and that he also asked him for the names of the commanders for the war crimes tribunal. And I would like to draw your attention to what you said, when you said that you have ruled, that that's what it says in the transcript. It says that in the transcript of Maisonneuve's testimony, and you can see that in the penultimate quotation of Maisonneuve in the document that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you hold a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, the Chamber would like you to lead the evidence in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. Questioned by Mr. Kay:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Colonel Petrovic reported to you was said at the meeting? And if you could take it item by item. What was his report to you of the meeting with Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Well, that the meeting took its chronological order. When they arrived, the questions that were discussed first and foremost: The place of the army, why the army was there, although the army had already been there throughout the summer, from 1998, the whole of 1998, from the month of April onwards; that the army had come out to Stimlje unlawfully, and before that, in January, we had control -- I think on the 4th or 5th of January -- was the last control made by Maisonneuve, who was in Stimlje and who saw and was satisfied with the numerical strength. And he asked, now why should the army be there in Stimlje? He said that it had come in there illegally, unlawfully. And I remember the major questions that were raised, and they were this: Whether the army went into Racak, and where the front line was, whether they had gone into Racak. And as allegedly during that period of time, he said that there was a major crime that had been committed, he asked for the names of the commanders, to see who the commanders were, higher ranking and lower ranking, in the village who had perpetrated that crime. That's what I remember now without any written trace of that or aide-memoire, because it's been six years since that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want any explanation, but I just want you to now tell us what Petrovic reported to you he said to Maisonneuve at that meeting. Without any explanation, just what he reported to you he said to Maisonneuve.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Well, his words were this -- of course, depending on the questions. I cannot give you his words word-for-word. But he answered the questions raised, and the questions raised were the ones I have just presented; that is to say, when he was asked those questions, he responded and answered them. He said that the army did not go into that area, that it was in Stimlje legally, that it did not enter the village of Racak, that he cannot give any names, name any names, because he didn't know who was there, who went there. He wasn't the person who was in command; he was the person who was informed. He didn't see anybody enter himself and wasn't able to provide that information. So Petrovic's answers followed the questions asked him by Mr. Maisonneuve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, move on. We have extracted the information that we wanted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I would like to have something stressed here, Mr. Robinson, an emphasis. You have it in the one-but-last line of the original of the record by Maisonneuve in English, where he says the following: "Regarding Petrovic [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] need names of commanders for war crime tribunal." [Interpretation] I'd like to draw your attention, gentlemen, to the fact that Walker, since this meeting was at 1037 hours, as it says in Maisonneuve's report, that Walker, only on the 16th in the afternoon hours, arrived in Racak and was astounded when he allegedly saw that a massacre had been -- some sort of massacre had been perpetrated there. So Maisonneuve, before Walker had allegedly uncovered this massacre and the bodies in the ravine, in the gully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We haven't yet reached the stage for closing speeches. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is a very useful document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your unit was the only unit there. General Maisonneuve, on 5843 page of the transcript, said that the army said that the police was involved in Racak, which was obvious to them because the army could see the police from the hill, supporting them, and that at one of the meetings with Petrovic, a liaison officer of the 243rd Brigade, said that MUP had carried out the operation with the help of the army, deploying at least one tank and several Praga vehicles. Now, did Petrovic tell him that the MUP had perpetrated that action with army support?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic never informed me of anything like that, nor did the army enter there, nor did it go into action with MUP there. It neither had authorisation to do so, nor a plan, nor a written order issued. And the army could have partially seen this when the MUP entered Racak because it is right next to the area where the army was deployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness of the opposite side over there, Barney Kelly - I assume he's an investigator of theirs - testified about the events in the village of Racak, and said that on the 15th of January, the Serb forces carried out a massacre. Now, you had your unit in the close vicinity of the area. Do you have any information at all about what he says here, that the Serb forces executed the massacre?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No information that a massacre had been carried out. The knowledge of the commander on the area, the commander of the combat group, and my knowledge, pursuant to his reports, is that the forces of MUP engaged in counter-terrorist operations and that they engaged in combat with terrorists in the village. Now, how many wounded and dead there were, casualties on both sides, we didn't know because we didn't have that kind of information. It was only later that we learned, first of all from the information media and then through other information, about the casualties, if they were the right figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, Nasret Shabani, a witness from Racak, said that from the summer of 1998, the police and army were on the hills surrounding Racak, in the hills around Racak. Tell us why. What was happening in Racak itself? Was anything happening in the surrounding wooded area? And his testimony is on pages 6268 of the transcript, 6269.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that there was a strong communication line which in the summer period was very burdened with military movement from Stimlje to Dulje and further on. In view of the communication lines - and I've already spoken about them - on the territory of Kosovo, about 40 per cent had been cut off. Everything was done to cut off the Stimlje-Dulje route. And it was cut off during an operation when six of my soldiers, on the 14th of June, were wounded in a column which was in the rear and a logistics column to supply the units in the field. That's when the communication lines were cut off. And one month later, through a joint action, joint operation on the part of both the army and the MUP, pursuant to permission given by the superior command, or the corps command, in fact, the road was deblocked and it was taken up on both sides of the road, left side and right side, by positions of the MUP at a distance of 500 to 700 metres from the road itself on the elevations above the road, and there was constant patrolling through the ravine, the gorge. The army also had control of the gorge. In Racak, as we received information that there were -- the 161st Brigade there of the KLA, that they were there, on the basis of a command and information -- or, rather, that that part of the command had between 80 and 120 men --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in Racak itself?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Racak itself. They weren't units, they were citizens bearing arms, who had weapons with them. They weren't an army with its rules -- governed by rules and regulations. They were just based on some tribal village organisation. So from that area, there were constant attacks launched on the communication route, on the roads. And the army and the police were in the hills but not around Racak. Racak is lower down in the valley. But around Crnoljevo village. That's the only village in the gorge, and it maintained control of the gorge. And all the attacks were launched, to all intents and purposes, from Racak, from Belince, from Rance and Zborci, which is more northerly from that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This same witness, Nasret Shabani said that there were three or four conflicts between the KLA and Serb army and police and four attacks on the village prior to the events of the 15th of January; is that true? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I never heard about it, and I would have known had there been attacks on Racak either by the police or the army. It is possible that the police, independently working -- working independently of us, of course, that it went in to search for criminals, and that is within its remit. But the army never entered there, neither before the war, in 1998, rather, or throughout 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including that 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That's right. The army never entered that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "should have known." You said a moment ago in response to Mr. Bonomy's question, that your unit was about 1 kilometre away from Racak.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the unit that had been there all the time from April 1998 until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness Shukri Buja spoke about Racak. He stated that in December 1998 the KLA started digging bunkers. In Racak, the fortifications had not yet been ready at that time and were not used until the 15th of January. Did you know anything about those fortifications, where they were located and whether they were used?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: We in the army knew that wherever the terrorists were, they had fortifications. We didn't know about specific fortifications. I'm talking about us in the army. And we were not aware of whether they were used before, on, or after the 15th of January. It is unlikely that they were able to dig on the eve of the 15th of January, in view of the high altitude, winter conditions, frost. They must have been dug out during the summer and were only improved later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same witness said that, on the 15th of January, when the attack began, the KLA had 47 men in Racak.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your information about the strength of the KLA was --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Between 80 and 120.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says 47. Witness Agron Mehmeti from Racak stated that on the 27th -- on the 25th of July, 1998, there was an offensive against Racak. Your unit was nearby in the village you showed on the map. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, there was no action, no offensive. But he did mention a correct date. The road was freed on the 25th of July. The terrorists were expelled, after the road had been blocked for more than a month and a half. On the 25th of July, we managed to unblock the road. It's true that this operation took place, but it was 1 or 2 kilometres away from Racak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We don't have many documents from that time, but there is one, issued by you. General Jelic, tell us about the document marked as your report. Let me direct you. That's tab 17. Let us look at it. It's your document, isn't it? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That's my document, my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described several events. It says, among other things, that the report refers to the implementation of NP&P.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That means training, plan, and programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says that on the 14th of January, 1999, a unit from Dulje was carrying out regular TOT.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That's tactical training, topic 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now look at this. Your report is dated the 17th of January.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Addressed to the Pristina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's an original, contemporaneous document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this tank company did its training on the 14th. We won't go through the entire document. We're not interested in the 14th. Fourth paragraph of your report reads -- won't you read it yourself. On the 15th, that is the notorious 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: "On 15th January, 1999, the unit from the Dulje sector carried out regular tactical training, topic 9, training for 'a mechanised platoon on the march' along the trig point 915 - Ljubovce village - trig point 988 - Garamele - Rance village axis -" Rance village being trig point 1027 - "and back. "In the course of regular training along the above-mentioned axis, heavy infantry and mortar fire was opened from the Rance village sector (700 metres to the west - Dara Glava), and mortar fire from Rance village itself. Fire was returned from infantry weapons and a 12.7 millimetre anti-aircraft gun targeting the Dara Glava feature, crushing the terrorist group. The unit reached a point 500 metres outside Rance village (trig point 1027) and without any further fighting or shooting, it returned to the camp ground. It was impossible to get to the village of Rance because of the deep snow (about one metre deep). We did not enter any of the populated areas. "Our forces suffered no casualties."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your report for the 14th and the 15th.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It describes all that your unit did on those two days.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, activities on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including those training activities that have nothing to do with Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: This training was approved by the schedule and plan, and they were performed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So further on, you mention MUP.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: "In the early morning hours of the 15th of January --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on, at what time was the training exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 14th and the 15th. The report follows the chronological order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At what time of the day on the 15th was it taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Training starts usually at 8 a.m. and is over by 3, 4 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the troops who were involved in that, were they different from those, the part of the combat group that was fired upon from Belince or south of Belince?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand you. The troops were conscripts serving their regular military service. We have part of commissioned officers and part of normal NCOs. So these troops were conscripts going through regular training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clear this up completely, to avoid any misunderstanding. Paragraphs first and second refer to the 14th and to the training activities of this unit, this combat group from Dulje sector.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that clear from what is written here?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: It is clear that this is combat training. The unit is not performing any combat activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you describe exactly which topic of the planned training it is, and you describe the training activity that the unit was involved in on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, on the 15th, the unit from the Dulje sector is involved in tactical training, topic 9, and you describe the axis along which they went: Ljubovce, Garamele villages, the Dara Glava feature that is mentioned. None of these places are anywhere near Racak.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: It is at least 6 kilometres away from Racak, where this last unit went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you describe the kind of combat training they underwent.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is written in the last paragraph for the 15th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My only concern was about the -- who these troops were, and the answer I was given was that there were conscripts, but it's not immediately obvious from the report that that was the case. That was all. That's the only reason I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, it says, "Unit from the Dulje sector," so that's the unit that came from the Dulje sector. And as every military unit, it has an active-duty batch of troops plus personnel, active-duty personnel, and conscripts. And this unit was one company strong. The entire unit from Dulje was one company strong, and what is involved here is only one part of that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Jelic, Dulje is located in Suva Reka, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's north of Suva Reka, about 15, 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the municipality of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, that's about Dulje village, but we were on Dulje pass. It's a curve on the road overlooking Dulje village, about a kilometre, a kilometre and a half away maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that area also covered by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's here [indicates], Suva Reka, the territory of Suva Reka, the municipality of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did your zone of responsibility also cover that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said at the outset it was the zone of responsibility of the brigade. The right boundary of the area was from Prevalac, Sara mountain, Jezerske mountains, until Dulje, until this pass here, this curving line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it was there from April 1998 until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The document we're looking at talks about an educational training programme and combat training of combat group. The evidence you've given so far is that your combat group had two subgroups; one was based in Stimlje and the other one was based south of Dulje, in the area of Birac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to know is where the troops who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were training in the area of Rance came from. Which of the two subgroups did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command of the unit, and that was a mechanised battalion, as I said, had this combat group under its command. This combat group was on Dulje, and everything is related to Dulje. Then, in order to implement the training programme, part of the units involved in this training receive an assignment pursuant to the training programme. They get their schedule, the commanding officers are prepared, and then the training goes forward, like in any country of the world. The training is sometimes theoretical, sometimes practical, but mostly practical. They have to go out into the field and do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, perhaps you didn't understand the question, or I'm completely at sea on this. Did I misunderstand you when you said that your combat group was divided into two subgroups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It had two permanent standing subgroups, and you put it correctly; from an area overlooking Stimlje and the area of Birac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So my question then was: The group that was training in the area of Rance came -- or was part of which of the two subgroups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't have training in the area of Rance but from Dulje. It says here very specifically, trig point 915, that's Dulje; Ljubovce, trig point 988, I can show it to you on the map. That's here. [Indicates]. That's where the training was carried out. From Dulje, without going into populated areas in order not to upset the population, in order not to provoke anyone into moving out or opening fire, but training has to go on, even during the winter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're obviously not understanding the question. It must be my way of putting it to you. But I understood that the combat group was based in Dulje, in general, but was divided into two subgroups, one of which was in Stimlje and the other of which was south of Dulje, in Birac. Now, why is it not possible to identify from which of these came the people who were engaged in this training exercise and who actually were attacked from Rance village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not in dispute at all. Their base was the combat group Dulje, and from that base they went on training and returned. The previous day, they went in the opposite direction, to the north, and on day two, they went to the east. That's here in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's not clear to me, but I can take it no further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This training on the 14th and the 15th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- was not close to Racak. How close was it to Racak? What is the closest point they reached to Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Sixteen kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the nearest they got to Racak during the training.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the penultimate paragraph in your report, or the last paragraph. What does it say about the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: "In the early morning hours of 15 January 1999, forces of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia set up a blockade in the general area of Racak village and the Hadovic quarter at about one kilometre west of Stimlje, the purpose of which was to search for terrorists who had been shooting at MUP forces on the previous days. The strength and composition of combat forces were unknown."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought something else was written, but you're right, it says "composition."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I'll go on: "At around 0700 hours on the 15th of January, heavy infantry fire was opened at MUP forces from the surrounding peaks, hills and villages. Part of Combat Group 1 is in the general area of Stimlje, Canovica Hill ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what you showed on the map?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Right. "... where they are engaged in regular combat training, topic 1, 'daytime and night-time reconnaissance from a combat vehicle.' "After combat operations and an attack by Siptar sabotage and terrorist forces started, the unit occupied the sectors and took up the following positions for a flexible defence: 122-millimetre Howitzer artillery battery at about 1 kilometre south-west of Canovica Hill --" I can show it on a map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's all around Canovica Hill, where they were stationed.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Right, and a tank platoon at about 1 kilometre south-east of Canovica Hill. "... one anti-aircraft defence platoon in the trig point 671 sector ... a reinforced reconnaissance platoon at trig point 637, by the road ..." That's what I marked on the map by the road, a unit that controlled traffic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does it say further below?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: South to Belince village, "fire was opened from infantry weapons, a 12.7 millimetre Browning anti-aircraft machine-gun, an 82-millimetre mortar or mortars. Fire was opened on the combat group deployment sector. Fire was returned from a Praga ... and a 12.7-millimetre anti-aircraft gun. After firing back at the south sector of Belince village ... the shooting stopped. "Our forces suffered no casualties; all units are in full combat-readiness. "Artillery was not fired. Artillery pieces were not fired from." A search was conducted around Racak and the surrounding villages. "None of our vehicles entered either the village of Racak or any of the surrounding villages. "MUP forces set up a blockade and searched the village of Racak and the surrounding villages and then returned to base at 1600 hours." Witness Shukri Buja claims otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it's on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Witness Shukri Buja said there were KLA forces inside and that's why the army took up positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the matter of production of material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- I have some further information, and I'm likely to have more before the Court rises. May I have a couple of minutes at the end of the session, after the witness has withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we have an order here by the commander, General Lazarevic, dated the 17th of January, 1999, sent to you. It says: "To the Commander of the 243rd Brigade," and that is to be found in tab 18. I hope you have tab 18 in front of you.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says that part of the forces of the combat group -- well, I don't want to recount what it says here and give my own precis, but what does it say here? You tell us, in this order. And the date is the 17th of January.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order by the commander of the Pristina Corps in which he sends to my own person an order in order to create conditions for the MUP forces to enter the villages of Racak and Rance in order to investigate, as planned, the alleged killing of civilian population: "... I hereby issue the following order: Part of the forces of Combat Group 1 is to support an attack by two MUP platoons on the axis of the villages of Dulje-Ljubovce-Rance. The task is to rout the sabotage terrorist forces, DTS, on the axis of attack by the MUP forces and to reach the Rance village sector. The commander of the MUP forces, Veljko Radenovic, will report to the commander of BG 243/1 --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's combat group, is it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, combat group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Combat group of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That's right. "-- at the command post in the Dulje sector at 0700 hours on the 18th of January, 1999. The attack will begin at 0800 hours on the 18th of January, 1999. "2. Part of the forces of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade are to support a diversionary attack by one MUP platoon -- or demonstrative attack by one MUP platoon -- from the area of the 1st Company of PGP in Pristina, on the axis of the villages of Kosare-Malopoljce. The task is to tie up the sabotage terrorist forces in the sector of trig point 657 (Bajrak) and the village of Malopoljce and prevent any interventions in the direction of the village of Racak. "MUP platoon commander Zoran Vukadinovic, is to report to the commander of the unit of the army of Yugoslavia at 0730 hours on the 18th of January, 1999, at the exit from the village of Stimlje, in the direction of Urosevac. "The attack will begin at 0830 hours on the 18th of January, 1999. "3. MUP forces are to be supported by two Pragas from the sector as follows: "Trig 637 south of Canovica Brdo to support the forces of the 6th CPJP -" PJP being the special police units - "and the other Praga to support the forces of the 7th company of the PJP from trig 688, south-east 500 to 700 metres," that is to say, "behind it." "The commander of the anti-aircraft platoon (-1) will report to the company commanders on the road, at the turn-off into the pinewood (encampment area) at 0730 hours on 18 January 1999."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the pinewood forest and the encampment area is the position of the units as designated by you.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Otherwise, it's a forest that is 30 years old. The trees there are protected. They're very tall pine trees, and was perfect for setting up a camp for the army, for all conditions. And this order referred to investigations -- to enable investigations to take place concerning the village of Racak. This was probably a request from the MUP, and the corps commander decided as follows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what does it say in point 6? Let's skip the rest of it. It says: "As the MUP forces are given support --"

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. "As the MUP forces are given support, take measures to protect the civilian population and to remove them from the zone of combat operations," that is to say, special care and attention should be paid to avoid any casualties on the civilian population that can be -- could be in the combat area, either in organised fashion or individually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now take a look at the following: We have here in tab 12, I think we have an order of yours, your order dated the 18th of January, in order to ensure conditions for the MUP forces to be able to enter. Or what does it say in tab 10? Commander of the 243rd Motorised Brigade, you wrote the order.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is an order of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the order by which you carry out the order from the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I issued this order pursuant to an order from the corps commander to define the details that weren't stipulated there, to ensure the proper carrying out of the task. This was written on the 18th of January, 1999, in order to provide -- "... secure conditions for the entry of MUP forces in the village of Racak, Rance village, in order to carry out an on-site investigation related to the alleged killing of civilians, I hereby order:" And then it says 1. Anyway, I stress -- I set out the assignments. And in the last point, I emphasise that: "During the operations, protect civilians from fighting." That is what I say. This was sent to the commander of Combat Group 1, since he was in charge of the operation there, and we see that the subgroups came under his composition, the composition of his unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is Combat Group 1 that was stationed at Dulje with the two subgroups which were emphasised and stressed by Mr. Bonomy, as he understood it.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That means we didn't bring in new forces from the garrison or from the barracks. There was no need for us to bring in other reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have gone through several exhibits now; tabs 17, 18, and 12. I think that the time has come for me to tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit those as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, take a look at what we have in tab 13 now, please. You compiled a report dated the 19th of January. What does that report refer to?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a report upon an assignment having been carried out. A report is sent to the command. First of all, a short analysis is undertaken, and then a report is written about the assignment carried out. Here it is addressed to the command corps, the date is the 19th of January, about support to MUP units in overcoming and routing the sabotage and terrorist forces in the villages of Rance and Racak, which was the assignment given. And this is what it says in the report, under number 1: "On the 19th of January, 1999, between 0800 hours and 1730 hours, when overcoming the sabotage and terrorist forces, the MUP forces were supported as follows --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and then it goes on to list what the support was.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This report is based on the order given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the facts and figures, it says: "No significant resistance was given by the terrorist forces, sabotage terrorist forces." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And when we searched the terrain, an insignificant number of equipment was found; 30 loaves of bread, which means that quite a large group was there, and a calculator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now let's take a look at another of your documents in tab 14. We'll go back to the state border and that question. What does this document refer to? And the date is the 26th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my order dated the 26th of January, for laying mines as obstacles at critical places along the state border. "Order: Pursuant to the order of the Pristina Corps command ... and in order to prevent illegal border crossings, I hereby order: "1. The Temporary Officer for Border Affairs of the 243rd Motorised Battalion, in cooperation with the Command of the 57th Border Battalion shall compile --" and they secured the border towards Macedonia -- "shall compile a plan of touring the state border and laying obstacles along the state border in accordance with the order of the Pristina Corps Command strictly confidential ..." that was issued on 14 January 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the reasons for these letters to be undertaken? What activities were you reacting to here? What was this response of yours to?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: As I said, the state border was a newly formed state border, just three or four or five years old. It was an undefined border towards Macedonia. Globally speaking, it was defined, but not its individual sections. People had land there, and citizens were issued provisional permits. However, permits to travel to one or the other side were abused. There was abuse of border crossings and there was black marketeering along the border belt. As they were under sanctions for economic reasons, there was increased contraband, and weapons were brought in, especially from the western region of Macedonia, that is from the Tetovo area. The units which provided security for the state border here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for the purposes of those who do not know about this, there's a concentration of Albanian population, the Albanian inhabitants in Macedonia in that area.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since we provided line security for the border belt - that's the way we do it - the units who were in depth, providing security there, had the technology, necessary technological equipment, and were reinforcements for the line security. But nevertheless there were places that you could not secure well enough around the clock, 24 hours. And in view of the configuration of the terrain there, Mount Sara, which is an altitude -- the highest peak is over 2.000 metres -- or over 1.500 metres, where you have snow until the month of May, heavy snow there, and the contraband routes were never defined but were changed constantly. This meant that we had to set up obstacles on the basis of joint cooperation with the officials from the state border, the units in depth providing security there, and the battalion, and to inform the soldiers patrolling the area where the mines had been laid so as to prevent self-wounding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, tell us what this next document contains, tab 15. That, once again, is one of your orders. Does it describe the situation and problems that you were encountering at that time, in a way?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is indeed my order. The unit, having the rank of a brigade, several thousand men, is a live organism, and there are always problems that occur in a unit of that size. Of course, it is normal that the brigade command analyses the situation and takes steps and measures to prevent any untoward events from taking place, especially where it comes to providing security for the border belt in depth. I'd like to read out a few passages from this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This "V/D" means extraordinary events; is that right? "Vanredni dogadjaj"?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, with adverse consequences to the brigade units, jeopardise morale and despite -- go to the detriment of irreparable damage of the reputation of the army of Yugoslavia, and blemishes the image of the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say happened here?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Well, in January there were two fires. Several weapons were burnt down, pieces of personal equipment and protection equipment. This is January. Low temperatures. According to the previous order, we saw that we issued orders to the units that they should not be in private buildings. There were tents where the soldiers had been put up, and so there were fires that broke out in the tents when fires were lit, which led to damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also casualties on the part of the soldiers, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the most frequent causes of this, in view of the fact that the unit was in the field for months, over-exertion, fatigue on the part of the men that were engaged in these combat operations, upsets the conduct of the individuals concerned, lowers the concentration level and makes them less capable of carrying out their assignments. Because if a young man of 18 years old, for example, has spent months in trenches, outside proper building facilities, it is quite normal that they suffer from fatigue, which means that the level of concentration drops and efficiency drops. Fires break out as accidents, there are other accidents, and so on and so forth. That is why this order was written in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General. Let me just have a look now. Paragraph 63(k), that paragraph pertains to alleged deportations. It is claimed here that in the Kacanik municipality -- let me just stop at this point. The municipality of Kacanik, as you explained, is in your area of responsibility; right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the municipality of Kacanik, "Between March and May 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked villages in the Kacanik municipality and the town of Kacanik itself. This attack resulted in the destruction of houses and religious sites, including, but not limited to, the mosques of Kotlina and Ivaja." You're the commander of those troops in the area. Can you say something about these allegations?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Kacanik is the seat of the municipality. MUP forces were always there. And after mobilisation was carried out, and after decisions were passed, it was also taken up by the army of Yugoslavia. At the time that you referred to here, in view of the presence of the MUP in the town itself and all structures, namely, hospitals, the Municipal Assembly, et cetera, were functioning and they were in the hands of the legal and legitimate authorities. It is illogical for the army to attack the town of Kacanik, because practically they would be attacking themselves this way. Kacanik was never held by anyone else except for the official state authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is nonsense, is it, that Kacanik was attacked. And what about this, where it says, "Villages in the municipalities were attacked," so we shall skip over the town of Kacanik. The houses were destroyed, religious sites, including the mosques in Kotlina and Ivaja?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: As for the mosques in Kotlina and Ivaja, I really never heard of anyone having destroyed these religious sites, nor was there any need to enter these villages. Now, I'm just talking about the military at this point in time. The army never entered these villages. They were engaged in anti-terrorist fighting, starting from the NATO aggression on the 24th of March, since the area of responsibility of the brigade was immediately attacked, that the 162nd Brigade of the so-called KLA was there, which kept attacking units in the defence areas, because by the 24th we had established the defence completely, and every battalion-level unit had own intervention unit. And this intervention unit practically defended the combat order of that battalion. The objective of this unit was not to have heavy equipment revealed, not to have artillery, tanks, and APCs moved, because in that way they would be discovered by NATO forces and therefore would be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this paragraph that deals with alleged deportations, that is, paragraph 63(i), it says that: "On the 8th of March, 1999 -" or around that date - "the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -" that is you, on the spot - "attacked and partly burned the village of Kotlina," and that on the 24th -- on the 24th of March, 1999, they attacked Kotlina again using heavy equipment, and that is why many men fled into the woods and women and children were ordered by the forces of the FRY and Serbia to board vehicles that then took them to Kacanik. Those that didn't manage to fit into these trucks had to walk to Kacanik. A certain number of male inhabitants of Kotlina were killed during the attack, including 17 men whose bodies were thrown into wells. Before leaving, the forces of the FRY and Serbia razed the rest of the village. That's what's written here. Please, are these allegations correct? This is your area of responsibility. What can you say about this? What have you got to add to this, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: These allegations are incorrect. On the 8th of March, the army did not enter any villages, nor was it engaged in any combat activity. On the 28th of February and the 8th of March, the forces of the MUP clashed with the terrorists of this 162nd Brigade. That's when Captain Staletovic was killed - I think that's what his name was - and four policemen were wounded. When searching for the terrorists, the MUP forces entered the village as they were looking for these terrorists on the basis of intelligence received, and they clashed with them. That's the information that I received when we exchanged information with the MUP and my unit, which was in the field. After all, the verifiers were there too, and they confirmed it as well. From the 24th of March onwards, what was characteristic for this area was that there were attacks in this area all the time against the units that were holding their positions in their area of defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was carrying out the attacks?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: The Siptar terrorist forces from the 162nd Brigade, which is stationed in that area, and probably the 163rd Brigade, which later grew into a brigade from the Nerodimlje operations zone. In this period, my units could not have entered a single village in view of the differences in altitude. Please take a look at the map and please see that the altitude is over 1.000 metres everywhere, and that basically this is a backwater. This is the area of Mount Sara. Very bad roads. There's snow. The units did not dare move so that their heavy equipment would not be discovered, so they only had the intervention units responding, if attacked. It's a bit strange for us to be transporting civilians. That would be absurd when, at the level of a company, you have one motor vehicle which is full of ammunition. Why would we unload ammunition in order to transport 18 persons, or let us even cram people in; 30 people. But it would have been insane for any commander to make that kind of decision and to leave its ammunition outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Apart from your forces, which you say were not involved in any attack on Kotlina, there would have been other forces of the FRY and Serbia in that area, wouldn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this area, my forces were the only forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, if we're talking about the army. All of them were under my command. And also there were the forces of the Republic of Serbia, which is the MUP. I have already said that the army never attacked Kacanik, and the MUP could not have attacked themselves either. As for the villages that are by the road where the combat groups are, which were under constant attacks, we then responded with fire from units that belonged to these groups. So if this is a battalion, they have a rapid deployment company that can prevent sabotage groups from disturbing the combat disposition. And we didn't dare move our heavy combat equipment because of surveillance from the air, where there was absolute supremacy. And in this way we would have become easy targets and everything would have been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I notice that the last passage of evidence is a report, and, on the witness's account, a synthesis of what he's been told by others, without explaining where or when he learnt about it. It would obviously help us all if we had some further detail of his sources at this stage rather than my having to go to every piece of evidence that I want to ask about and deal with it at a later stage, because that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was that in reply to my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, it was earlier on than that. He dealt -- he gave a general answer to the question about the paragraph in the indictment and said that this came to him from sources, but that's all we -- sources in the field --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, let us know the sources of the information that you had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sources of information are, first and foremost, the reports of my subordinates and my personal insight. It is my unit. I was not outside my area of responsibility. My headquarters were in Urosevac, and my forward command post kept shifting. Most often it was on the main axis of defence, south of Kacanik, near Djeneral Jankovic; actually where the situation was the most difficult in this period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 63(ii), that pertains to these alleged deportations, it says that on the 27th and 28th of March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 63(k)(ii).

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, 63(k)(ii).

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "On the 27th and 28th of March, 1999, or around that date, the forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the town of Kacanik. Forces of the FRY and Serbia harassed, detained, beat, and shot many Kosovo Albanian residents of Kacanik." So this is the 27th and the 28th of March, 1999. That's the allegation made here; that you went around Kacanik, that you were detaining people, beating them up, shooting them, the Kosovo Albanian residents. "Thousands of persons fled to nearby forests and eventually walked across the border into Macedonia. Other displaced persons from the town of Kacanik and nearby villages walked to the village of Stagovo, where they boarded trains that took them to the Macedonia border." These trains that took them seem to mean that somebody forced them to board trains. That's the context. So I've read this out to you, what it says here, what is written here in this paragraph, and what pertains to the 27th and 28th of March in Kacanik. What can you say about these allegations?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: I think that these allegations are incorrect. Kacanik was never attacked. And I repeat: There was no necessity to attack Kacanik, because MUP forces were in it all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already said that.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: All state institutions were functioning, so there was no need to attack the town itself. I know, I had reports during this period of time, that sometime toward the end of February, not the end of March, a police patrol had been attacked in town, and that patrol had four or five persons wounded and one person was killed. The MUP took measures to find the perpetrators, or rather, to destroy this terrorist group. And since this had to do with the town itself, after midnight they were expelled, or rather, they fled from Kacanik to the east, to these forests. I only know of that incident in the town of Kacanik. There was no harassment. The army had its positions in front of Kacanik throughout the war, from the 24th, that is. We took the areas for defence prior to the aggression, and we were present, we were there. We could not attack the MUP forces, because in this way we would practically be destroying ourselves. Or if we were to attack Kacanik, we could attack some of our own forces too, our own army forces, and that's absurd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you say to this: That thousands of persons fled to nearby forests and eventually walked across the border into Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: So many people left, which is only natural when the military is area, when the border is nearby, when it is to be expected that NATO forces would come from Macedonia. And they were right by the border too, about 20.000 NATO troops, with two mechanised brigades, an armoured brigade. So these are elite units that were there. Who would be sitting there, waiting right by the road? Most of these people really moved out, but first and foremost out of fear from NATO aggression, because they are by the main road where army positions are. It was to be expected that the NATO aggression would take place there, that that's where the attack would be. People were afraid and they were leaving. Not only Kacanik but also other places. There are Serb villages there too, purely Serb villages, and the population went in the direction of Serbia and Macedonia, it depended. For example, Nerodimlje, Babus; these were predominantly Serb villages. And practically nobody stayed there. Regrettably, today there are no local people there. However, the media reported that NATO troops were there in Macedonia on the eve of the aggression, that they brought forces there, they knew that mobilisation was carried out, that units took up their positions, and what else could you expect but people being frightened and leaving the area? I think that these people were simply afraid, and that they were afraid even before this, and then they left. Although Kacanik was never totally empty. Thirty or 40 per cent of the residents stayed in town itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just a second. What was the ethnic composition of Kacanik at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kacanik was predominantly Albanian, ethnically speaking. The majority were Albanians, there were some Romas, some Egyptians, and a few percentage points of Serbs. I don't know about Montenegrins, but there were very few of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as for them going to Stagovo, they boarded trains there and then they were driven away to the Macedonian border. What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Driven away? That would mean that somebody brought in vehicles. In Stagovo, there is a train station. There are two trains per day, and they operated between Kosovo and Djeneral Jankovic. This must be the wrong word, the wrong term, "driven away." People would come there and board a train, but, I mean, why would they go to Stagovo, which is 4 or 5 kilometres away, when they could have boarded trains in Kacanik? Nobody was trying to stop anyone from leaving. And I say, yet again, that no army troops were transporting anyone. The army doesn't have any capacities for doing that. There are no vehicles that can transport passengers. It's for different purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So regular trains were used that go --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Twice a day. They were small; two, maybe four carriages, railway cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was the regular traffic.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, regular traffic. It goes just to the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing and back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no traffic across the Macedonian border.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they went to the last stop, which is the Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That's about a hundred metres away, or so, from the border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's a regular railway stop, railway station.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the border crossing is right next to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In this same paragraph, (k)(iii), it says: "On or about the 13th of April, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded the village of Slatina and the hamlet of Vata. After shelling the village, infantry troops and police entered the village and looted and burnt the houses. During this action, 13 civilians were shot and killed. Following this attack, much of the population of Slatina fled to Macedonia." At the beginning when you were showing these villages, you indicated Slatina as well as the hamlet of Vata. Can we see that on the map?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: It's this area. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This reference is to the 13th of April, on or about that date. Where was the combat deployment of your units in juxtaposition to Slatina and Vata?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: That's the village of Slatina and the hamlet of Vata. This was the combat deployment of one unit that actually took up their combat positions and was there on the eve of the 24th of March. That unit stayed there. It didn't enter the village. I just want to make one thing clear: The combat disposition of a unit is defined by three points, or four points if it's a larger unit. If we say that in this case it was Bicevac, Slatina, Banjica, that doesn't mean that the army goes into those three places. It just means that, geographically speaking and tactically speaking, the commander of the unit chooses the most favourable points around it to take up position, which means the army didn't go into these villages, but instead took up defence positions in a certain defence area. That means that the road from Globocica - that's this road here - which is a hard-surface road with a lot of serpentines, a very wooded area, heavily wooded area, with an intersection forking off to Strpce, or later on to Prizren. Attacks on all vehicles, mainly logistical vehicles, were frequent. What is typical here is that the command of my brigade, the 243rd Brigade, was based there. I think there is a symbol indicating it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If there was shelling by any army unit of Slatina, it would have been done by your unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if that had happened, but it wasn't possible in this case because we were already there. We couldn't shell ourselves. The distance was only 300, 400 metres. These positions were already prepared in engineering terms. Obstacles were put up, combat shelters. It was the so-called decisive defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you attacked from Slatina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were never attacked from any village in my brigade's area of responsibility. But those terrorist groups, as a rule, opened fire or attacked from clearings. They would fire several volleys from automatic weapons and disappear. We can only assume that if there were attacks on this road, where we indeed had casualties, that it was the residents of Slatina, Vata, Dubicevac, some other village, that were involved. We didn't capture anybody so we were unable to know. If we had captured somebody and checked their IDs, we would have known. What we knew was that it was the area where the 162nd Brigade was active. But it could also have been somebody from one of the other villages around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to remember, Mr. Nice, did you lead any evidence from any person from Slatina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't remember offhand, I'm afraid. If you give me a minute, I'll find it and let you know. I'm sure I can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I imagine if you did, then probably Mr. Milosevic would put that to the witness. Please carry on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This event was described, as I quoted, in 63(k)(iii), so it's one of those allegations made against me. Mr. Robinson, I'm going to ask the witness now about allegations related to a different place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time, around the 13th of April, in this area, Slatina, Vata, were there any other forces, apart from yours?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, no other troops except mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the police?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: There were no police there, unless they just went through Strbac, Kacanik, Urosevac. They could have used the roads that went through these places. They were not located there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the area of your responsibility, there was practically no police.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No, never. And speaking in principle, nobody else can be present within the combat deployment of an army unit in order to avoid all sorts of mistakes and confusion. Police or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no police within your area of combat deployment.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 13th of April and in that period, there was nobody in that area, apart from your army troops.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC
